national.title: Collins enlists Manchin to woo moderates as she distances herself from Trump
national.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins campaigned Wednesday with an unusual ally: Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin.
national.body: Lewiston, Maine — Republican Sen. Susan Collins is campaigning on a simple idea: She can sit across the table from anyone. On Wednesday, she did it literally, sharing breakfast sandwiches with Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin and a roomful of Maine voters as she makes her case to people of every political stripe."She's not a Trump senator. She's not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator," Manchin told reporters after dining with Collins in the morning. "She's an American senator that represents her state of Maine."Collins is the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state that President Trump lost. CBS News rates the race a toss-up. But Collins, who is running for a sixth term, has a history of surviving tough reelection battles and outrunning other Republicans. In 2020, she won by more than 8 points, even as Mr. Trump lost Maine by 9 points.Both Collins and Manchin — who represented deep-red West Virginia in the Senate before leaving the Democratic Party and retiring in 2024 — have a history of clashing with their respective parties.Collins worked to distance herself when pressed on Mr. Trump on Wednesday. While touring a local New Balance factory, she was asked about Trump envoy Steve Witkoff calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" for releasing a jailed U.S. citizen. The question drew a visible reaction from Manchin, who shook his head. Collins responded with a flat "no.""I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine," she said. She also said she does not support Mr. Trump's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia and strike a diesel deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, arguing it will give Russia more funding to attack Ukraine.Collins, who has long defected from parts of Mr. Trump's agenda, has also criticized the president's handling of the Iran war. In debates, she has said the president did not have a good plan and that the conflict should end. national.title: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
national.summary: Hotel chaos, transport mishaps and diplomatic blunders cast a spotlight on organisers and the firm hired to deliver the games.
national.body:
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.

There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".

Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.

"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.

The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.

Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.

Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds" .

Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.

national.title: NFL welcomes a review of how Eagles handled Jalen Hurts' blood clots, Roger Goodell says
national.summary: The NFL welcomes an investigation into the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots after the players' union asked for one, Commissioner Roger Goodell said Wednesday.
national.body:
Stephen Whyno, Associated Press Stephen Whyno, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — The NFL welcomes an investigation into the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots after the players' union asked for one, Commissioner Roger Goodell said Wednesday.

Goodell said in his news conference at the end of the NFL's annual fall meeting that Dr. Allen Sills, the league's chief medical officer, has gone through the steps that were followed and added that the union had a right to call for a review.

"Obviously, there was a medical evaluation, and I think our protocols were incredibly good there," Goodell said. "The protocols were followed. Our process is to make sure that's the case, and our chief medical officer has gone through that, so we're comfortable that what we've seen in the protocols have happened."

Sills on Tuesday offered a passionate defense of the Eagles medical staff. The NFL said officials were in touch with team doctors and trainers, as well as the Cleveland Clinic in London, where the Eagles were playing the Jaguars on Oct. 11.

League executive vice president Jeff Miller said officials had a good sense of the course of events, which included Hurts being evaluated at a hospital the day before the game. Miller disputed a report that Hurts was awake for more than 30 hours before playing against Jacksonville, saying that the 28-year-old returned to the hotel and slept for roughly seven or eight hours.

Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms.

Goodell downplayed the role that international travel may have had in the situation.

national.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
national.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
national.body:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".

Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.

The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.

New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.

national.title: Pope Leo won't need more treatment after cancer surgery, doctors say
national.summary: Pope Leo XIV will not need any further treatment after having lung cancer surgery, his doctors said in a statement.
national.body: Pope Leo XIV will not need any further treatment after having lung cancer surgery, his doctors said in a statement Wednesday.Test results confirmed that the pope's cancer was localized, Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope's physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, his surgeon, said in a statement."A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required," the doctors said.Leo's cancer diagnosis was revealed last week after he was admitted to a Rome hospital for what was initially described as a surgery to remove a lung nodule. The pontiff was diagnosed with the common cancer of lung adenocarcinoma, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during a procedure that lasted about 90 minutes.In an interview with Vatican News published over the weekend, Margaritora said the discovery of the malignant lung tumor was "entirely accidental." A small spot was found at the base of the lung during a routine exam, he said, adding that doctors wouldn't have found it if it was located a little higher up."The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance – not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora told Vatican News.On Saturday, four days after his surgery, the 71-year-old pope left the hospital and was greeted by a large crowd cheering for him. He delivered his traditional Sunday noon prayer at the Vatican, thanking the faithful for their prayers and the hospital staff for their care."This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are living with illness or infirmity," Leo said. "Now that I have overcome this delicate phase, as you know, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers."Leo is continuing his recovery at the Vatican and hosted his usual general audience Wednesday, waving from the popemobile to the large crowd of the faithful gathered in St. Peter's Square and blessing children raised up to him.The pope is expected to travel to South America in early November, the Vatican said.

national.title: Teacher who survived Oregon school shooting recounts playing dead
national.summary: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, says she was shot before she had "any chance to act."
national.body: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, is sharing a statement about her experience, saying the gunman shot her before she had "any chance to act."In the statement Wednesday, Drury recalled running to see what was happening outside her classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School before spotting the shooter."I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there," Drury wrote. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.""Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she continued. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again."Drury suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries from the Oct. 15 shooting that killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Another student, a 7-year-old, was also seriously wounded.The suspect was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school. Police said he shot through the school's locked doors before entering a special needs classroom and opening fire.The gunman was tackled by another teacher and fatally shot by an armed bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, who followed him into the school, according to police. Drury said Wednesday she was sharing what happened to her because "I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately.""I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she wrote.She thanked those who have supported her since the shooting, and said, "What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy."

national.title: U.S. ordering some staff to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
national.summary: The State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their family members to depart Saudi Arabia, following an uptick in attacks by Houthi militants.
national.body: The U.S. State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their family members to depart Saudi Arabia, following an uptick in attacks on the kingdom by Iran-backed Houthi militants.The department "issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote in a Wednesday X post, pushing back on a report that orders could apply to other Gulf states.CBS News has learned several other embassies adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, but have not gone on ordered departure, which involves the mandatory evacuation of designated diplomatic staff and accompanying family due to security risks.The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations. The decision to draw down personnel in Saudi Arabia comes after U.S. embassies in the kingdom, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries issued warnings over the weekend, urging Americans in the region to exercise caution and prepare for travel disruptions due to Houthi attacks."Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said Wednesday.The Houthis have launched drones and missiles at airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month that killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. One American was among those killed.The attacks have continued, with a Saudi-led military coalition reporting that it intercepted multiple Houthi drones on Monday and Tuesday.Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Tuesday that air defenses blocked a drone attack on the country's Shaybah oil field. Two people were killed and two were injured by falling debris, according to the agency, which did not specify who launched the drone.Meanwhile, the Houthis have sought to expand their territorial control in Yemen. national.title: Trump's political groups spend nearly $277 million in late midterm blitz on behalf of GOP candidates
national.summary: President Donald Trump's political groups have spent more than one-quarter of a billion dollars to bolster Republicans in the final stretch of this year's midterm elections, an unprecedented amount for a sitting president that underscores the stakes on Nov. 3.
national.body:
Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump's political groups have spent more than one-quarter of a billion dollars to bolster Republicans in the final stretch of this year's midterm elections, an unprecedented amount for a sitting president that underscores the stakes on Nov. 3.

"It's more than any president has ever spent, by far, on the midterms," said Corry Bliss, a GOP Senate and House campaign strategist who was the executive director of the Congressional Leadership Fund, House Republicans' super PAC in the 2018 campaign.

WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on how Trump's unpopularity is shaping the midterms

Trump had been under intense pressure to help Republican candidates as his party struggles to hold onto its slim majorities in the House and Senate. While the party in power almost always loses seats in midterm elections, Republicans are facing an especially challenging climb after Trump helped defeat several of the party's longtime incumbents and as he has been mired in low approval ratings amid deep voter frustration over persistently high costs and the unpopular war with Iran.

One bright spot for Republicans has been their huge financial advantage over Democrats this election cycle, aided by billionaires such as Elon Musk.

Trump-affiliated groups are now on track to spend potentially more.

Musk has also invested heavily in Texas, leading Talarico to accuse him of trying to buy the seat.

national.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
national.summary: Russia says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
national.body:
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.

Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.

The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.

Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."

The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.

national.title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces evacuations, shelter-in-place
national.summary: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
national.body: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal. One injury has been reported so far. According to officials, a Lucas County sheriff's deputy who responded to the scene wasn't feeling well and drove himself to a hospital. Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place due to a hazardous materials release."There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical, and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," said Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz. "As a result, our first responders and hazmat teams and safety teams are not approaching the tank." The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday. Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.Who is in the evacuation zone?According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.Meijer parking lot (off East Alexis) — Red Cross and TARTA buses are stationed to provide shelter as needed.The shelter-in-place zone is a 3-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. No injuries have been reported. Toledo public schools were closed on Wednesday.

national.summary: After special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing a U.S. citizen deemed to have been wrongfully detained, GOP Sen. John Cornyn responded, "No. Putin is a stone cold killer."
national.body: Washington — U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced immediate backlash Wednesday for praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" after he released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years and who had been determined to be wrongfully detained."You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin Wednesday in response to Hubbard's release. "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."Witkoff made the comment in St. Petersburg during a visit with the Russian president that was aimed at moving toward a resolution of the Ukraine war that Putin started four and a half years ago. Over the past month, Russia has been intensifying its strikes against civilian and energy infrastructure to try to cripple the power grid before the brutal Ukrainian winter. Mr. Trump was asked later in the day if he would describe Putin the same way Witkoff did. "Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out," Mr. Trump said during a White House roundtable on cyber crime. "But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other." Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment sparked pushback from Republicans, some of whom have openly criticized the president and his administration in recent months. "WTF, Steve?" wrote North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis. "Look up the definition of 'humanitarian.' What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say. You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a 'humanitarian.'"Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas responded to a video of Witkoff's comments: "No. Putin is a stone cold killer," he wrote on X. "Another embarrassment," said Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the Trump administration's handling of Russia and Ukraine. Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, who has also been critical of the administration, was asked about the comment on the campaign trail and replied, "I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. national.summary: President Donald Trump will visit South Carolina on Wednesday to boost Graham, whose stumbles in her first campaign since replacing her late brother have Democratic voters hopeful — but not necessarily optimistic — that their candidate can break Republicans' grip on the state.
national.body:
PENDLETON, S.C. (AP) — President Donald Trump will visit South Carolina on Wednesday to boost U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, whose stumbles in her first campaign since replacing her late brother have Democratic voters hopeful — but not necessarily optimistic — that their candidate can break Republicans' grip on the state.

Although South Carolina is not typically a midterm battleground, Trump has been deeply invested in Graham. He supported her appointment to replace Lindsey Graham after his death in July, and he backed her in a special primary when she faced several more experienced Republican opponents. But some distance emerged between the Republican president and the senator over the weekend over his decision to waive Ukraine war sanctions on Russia that were set to be imposed under a law named after Lindsey Graham.

WATCH: Trump holds GOP midterm rally in battleground North Carolina

Republicans want to make sure Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee and a pediatrician, doesn't pull off an upset victory. More than $34 million has flowed into the race, and Republicans have hammered Andrews as a "radical liberal" and accused her of supporting surgeries for transgender minors, which she denies.

Trump this week is rallying every day for candidates across the country, even in conservative areas, and imploring voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot" in hopes of averting a lackluster midterm turnout for Republicans.

"Darline Graham knows that our campaign's momentum is so strong she called Donald Trump to come campaign for her in South Carolina," Andrews said in a fundraising appeal email.

Lindsey Graham had been on a glide path to a fifth term when he died of an aortic tear. Darline Graham, former director of the state agency for the blind, received bipartisan support when she was appointed to serve out her brother's term. But her decision to run for the seat in the midterms prompted skepticism that the political neophyte was up for the job.

Darline Graham had the endorsement of Trump, who campaigned for her before the runoff with U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman. A stumble over a question related to U.S. policy in Taiwan, in which Graham admitted she was "not that informed on national security," prompted questions over her readiness.

national.body:
Voters have record low trust in Republicans' ability to handle their top issues like immigration and rising prices, according to the latest Strength In Numbers/Verasight poll shared with NPR.

The poll also finds a strong majority of voters want the next Congress to undo President Trump's agenda — or act as a check on his power — on policies like tariffs and trade, health care and immigration.

Less than two weeks out from Election Day, voters say they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican by a double-digit margin among registered voters (52% to 41%) and likely voters (54% to 42%).

The survey of 2,028 respondents was conducted Oct. 13-19 and has a margin of sampling error of 2.2 percentage points, meaning results could be about 2.2 points higher or lower.

Trump's job approval sits at near-record lows for his second term, with just 34% approving of his performance and 62% disapproving, with 50% strongly disapproving.

"Trump's ratings hit new lows on seven of the 10 issues we've tracked since May 2025, from jobs and trade to immigration and border security, and he's now underwater on every issue we ask about," Morris said. "The president's policies have even harmed Republicans, with voters now more likely to say they trust Democrats to handle the issues of immigration and the economy."

Among adults, prices and inflation are collectively mentioned far and away as the most important problem facing the country today, with 63% of respondents saying it was one of their top three most important problems and 39% listing it first. Other top issues include jobs and the economy, health care, elections and democracy and immigration.

national.title: Pope Leo's tests show he needs no further treatment for lung cancer, his doctors say
national.summary: Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localized, the Vatican said in a statement Wednesday.
national.body:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment for lung cancer after follow-up tests confirmed the disease was localized, the Vatican said in a statement Wednesday.

Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed last week in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, four days after surgery and well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.

The pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the pope's surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread.

"A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the doctors said.

The pope had the lower section, or lobe, of his right lung removed to try to ensure that all the cancer was removed.

Additional treatment is offered in such cases if follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread or has certain other signs that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumors are caught very early, such as when someone has an X-ray or other scan that shows a spot long before it's large or causing symptoms.

The pope appears to have had one of those "incidental findings," a nodule in his lung spotted during another exam. In an interview with Vatican News, Margoritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome's Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations.

The pope carried on business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Putin, and has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St. Peter's Square and Wednesday's longer audience, when he greeted the faithful from all over the world.

national.title: US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
national.summary: The 74-year-old former teacher, who was captured in 2022, has been released without any "swap" required, Trump says.
national.body:
Russia has released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.

Stephen Hubbard had been taken to the city's Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday.

President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary". Following the release, Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian".

Hubbard, who was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, was accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine when he was captured in 2022, shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion.

CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.

Witkoff praised Putin for releasing Hubbard, saying: "You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian - you are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you."

His comments sparked a backlash from lawmakers in the Republican Party, with Representative Don Bacon posting on social media that it was "another embarrassment". Senator John Cornyn said Putin "is a stone cold killer".

In response to a question from the BBC about the backlash, Vice-President JD Vance said Witkoff's "job is to go over there and get a job done".

national.title: Ex-prosecutor charged with treason in Mexico over US drug raid
national.summary: César Jáuregui Moreno is accused of allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April.
national.body:
Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation.

César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year.

The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers.

Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations.

The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday.

A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports.

Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country.

national.body:
Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.

national.summary: A growing share of American families are having to shell out more than $2,000 a month for childcare services, new data shows.

national.summary: The verdict should be seen as a warning for tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.
national.body:
Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press

A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy, in what marks the largest fine ever against the owner of Facebook.

The verdict should be seen as a warning for tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.

"This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said.

Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go toward state education spending.

"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," said Torrez, who acknowledged that the money would be tied up as Meta appeals.

Representatives for Meta, which previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict, didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment about the amount. The Menlo Park, California-based company was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon and its shares were trading 2% higher following the penalty announcement.

In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida -- to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.

national.title: Top 2 Democrats on Intel say they're preparing for Trump to claim foreign meddling
national.summary: The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees said they are working under the presumption that the president will seek to justify election interference by alleging fraud.
national.body:
The top Democrats on the House and Senate intelligence committees say they are operating under the presumption that President Trump and his allies will allege fraud related to this year's midterms in order to justify election interference.

"We start with the premise that the president is going to do that. It would be irresponsible not to, speaking as somebody who was in the chamber on January 6, 2021," said Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn. "We're making the assumption that the president is not going to accept the results of what looks to be a very challenging election for him and his party."

Speaking alongside Himes on Wednesday, Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, said that one way the president could do that: claiming foreign interference in the voting process.

"President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis in a statement to NPR. "While extreme Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive action to protect our elections including prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion."

Asked if he would accept the results of the election by a reporter earlier this month, Trump replied, "What do you think? Of course I will, but we don't want cheating."

Only on NPR How Democrats in Congress are preparing for Trump midterm election interference Himes and Warner are members of the Gang of Eight, senior lawmakers who oversee the nation's spy agencies and receive confidential briefings.

In a briefing for reporters, Warner and Himes said they have made clear to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and other intelligence leaders that they must be immediately reachable by phone on and after Election Day in the event that Trump alleges foreign interference in the election. Or, Himes said, if the president "decides to use allegations of foreign interference as an excuse to seize ballot boxes, question the validity of the election."

"If, at noon on Election Day, the president announced that the Iranians have undertaken operation," Himes said, "I'm on TV saying 'I'm Gang of Eight and I have received no such briefing, no such information, and I have no reason to believe that this is accurate.'"

national.summary: The wife of a diplomat based in Abuja travelled to Kampala for a vacation.
national.body:
Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.

The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return.

The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said.

"Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.

local.title: Busy Bee, other West Main storefronts to get refresh
local.summary: The projects are part of a $10 million revitalization effort paid for by the state and the Ralph C. Wilson Foundation.
local.body:
Storefronts along West Main Street in Rochester are getting a refresh, part of a $10 million revitalization effort.

Among those slated for an upgrade are Morse Lumber and Busy Bee Restaurant . Grant funds also will help repair and reopen shuttered buildings along the corridor between Genesee Street and South Plymouth Avenue, including prepping the space immediately to the west of Busy Bee for a future café.

A total of 22 projects have been awarded grants ranging from $25,000 and $250,000 to cover up to 90% of eligible expenses. Funding for the project comes from New York state and the Ralph C. Wilson Foundation.

"This investment reflects what’s possible when government, philanthropy, businesses, and community organizations come together around a shared vision," Mayor Malik Evans said in a statement.

Evans joined others for a ceremonial groundbreaking on Wednesday outside Rochester Jewels , a nonprofit mentoring organization at 174-178 W. Main St. serving school-aged girls. That building is getting roof and window repairs. Grants also can be used for machinery and equipment, and improvements to public spaces. There are developing plans for public art and amenities to be added to the area, which officials said could leverage additional funding.

Busy Bee Restaurant, which has been downtown since the 1930s, and at its 124 W. Main St. location since the 1980s, will celebrate its grand re-opening on Monday. The building is slated to get a refreshed storefront and awning, as well as other work on the masonry, windows and drainage, while the upper floors are prepped for housing. Morse Lumber will see similar facade, siding and window improvements, pressure washing, painting and new signage, officials said.

local.title: History buff's gift will double historic preservation grants in greater Rochester next year
local.summary: Don Hall donated nearly his entire estate to the Rochester Area Community Foundation's historic preservation fund, which he established in 2006
local.body:
The Rochester Area Community Foundation says a recent gift will allow the organization to double its historic preservation grantmaking next year.

The $2.73 million gift came from the estate of former Strasenburgh Planetarium director Don Hall, who established the RACF historic preservation fund in 2006.

The program awards grants to local projects that restore historic buildings and digitize historic material.

Marty Hartstein, the Community Foundation's director of donor engagement and impact, said Hall was a man of relatively modest means who had a passion for history. And he wanted people to know they did not have to be wealthy to become a philanthropist.

"You know, his salary when he retired was at $60,000," Hartstein said. "Giving back was something that he made space for, and he definitely wanted to serve as that model to others."

Twenty-eight local nonprofits received historic preservation grants from the fund in 2026.

Hall, who died at age 85 last November, donated almost his entire estate to support historic preservation in the Rochester region, according to Hartstein. He had a passion for cemeteries, tombstones, and the mansions along East Avenue.

The program hopes to also expand people's understanding of what historic preservation is, said RACF senior program officer Annette Jimenez Gleason.

Brian Meyer started with some suggestions. He proposed a 10% discount for people who pay property taxes early. City officials have floated the id
local.body:
Several Dunkirk residents complained and offered ideas about the proposed 2027 city budget, and its 11% tax increase, at Tuesday's Common Council meeting.

Brian Meyer started with some suggestions. He proposed a 10% discount for people who pay property taxes early. City officials have floated the idea of requesting, or demanding, earlier tax payments as a way to help the city's springtime bottom line.

"You gotta give somebody an incentive," he said. "If you give me 10%, I'll be there to pay my taxes on Jan. 3. If you aren't going to give me any incentive, I'm going to wait until the end."

Meyer, who runs Dunkirk's flea market, added that the city needs to do a better job of putting surplus machinery up for auction. He said leaf pickup should be canceled, as only the First and Second Wards really benefit from it. His final suggestion was that city employees who live outside of Dunkirk should pay a 10% tax on their salaries.

Robert Whittemore, a city Planning Board member who spoke for himself, said his interest in Dunkirk affairs began in late 2024 with a proposed 108% tax increase. That wound up at 84%.

"I decided to attend as many different meetings as possible to understand why and how this happened," Whittemore said. "While there are many reasons for this, it is not helpful to continue to blame. We definitely need to come together as a city to fix our problems. Public hearings are one place to do that, as well as contacting our officials. ...We need to make our voices heard. This doesn't mean we always get what we want, but if we don't say anything, it surely won't happen."

Candy Smathers said she "had a gripe about this tax issue. By the way, I see our mayor (Kate Wdowiasz) isn't here. I would like to invite Missy Mayor to come on down and do her job. Show up! She's supposed to be here. That upsets me quite a bit that she's not (here). I feel like she's bilking the community."

Wdowiasz famously declared earlier this year that she would no longer attend council meetings, claiming they had a "do-nothing" attitude and didn't really want to work with her. The mayor ended that hiatus a couple months later but has missed several council meetings since, including Tuesday's.

local.summary: A 19-year-old from Massachusetts faces expulsion in contested account.
local.body:
An RIT student is facing a felony charge for allegedly placing a recording device in the bathroom of a college residence hall.

Rochester Institute of Technology Public Safety discovered the device on Sunday, and notified the Monroe County Sheriff's Office. Deputies then began working to determine who was responsible for the unlawful recording, and to identify victims.

Investigators think the device was set up Friday evening. Working with RIT, they identified Avery E. Bird, 19, of Gloucester, Massachusetts, as a suspect and arrested him on Tuesday.

Bird faces a felony charge of second-degree unlawful surveillance.

local.title: GLYS WNY to purchase iconic Allentown building for LGBTQ+ community hub
local.summary: An iconic building in Buffalo’s Allentown district will become a hub for the region’s LGBTQ+ community, with GLYS WNY purchasing the former Oxford Pennant headquarters and workshop.
local.body: An iconic building in Buffalo’s Allentown district will become a hub for the region’s LGBTQ+ community, with GLYS WNY purchasing the former Oxford Pennant headquarters and workshop.According to a press release, the building at 810 Main Street will serve as the permanent home of GLYS WNY and the Pride Center of Western New York. Both organizations currently lease space at separate locations that cannot meet growing demand for their programs and services.“Finally, we will have a space for everyone,” said Ed Drantch, chair of the GLYS Board of Directors. “This begins a whole new chapter in our history.”The release states that the property includes 8,000 square feet of office space and a 5,000-square-foot former manufacturing facility. The purchase also includes more than 25 dedicated parking spaces at the adjacent 8 Street Louis Place.“The possibilities are enormous,” said Jack Kavanaugh, executive director of GLYS WNY. “Not only will we have a fully accessible building for all of our programs, we will also have room to grow and community space for groups who share our goals and values.”According to the release, several LGBTQ+ organizations have expressed interest in using the space, including the Nickel City Treble Makers, Buffalo Gay Men’s Chorus, Upstate Black Latino Pride and the Buffalo-Niagara LGBTQ History Project.The planned purchase and renovation are expected to cost more than $3 million, the release reads. James Zawodzinski Jr., a GLYS board member, is chairing a 25-person committee tasked with raising funds for the project.“This will better serve our youth, better serve our seniors and everyone in between,” said Zawodzinski.The new location is intended to provide expanded space for GLYS WNY and the Pride Center of Western New York while creating opportunities for other organizations to offer programs, build partnerships and serve the region’s LGBTQ+ community, according to the release.

entertainment.title: ‘Street Fighter’ Director Kitao Sakurai Built a Career by Embracing the Ridiculous
entertainment.summary: Sakurai helped launch ‘The Eric Andre Show’ in the 2010s, a building block that has now led to a big-budget video game movie.
entertainment.body:
Logo text In 1999, demonic rollerblading triplets armed with hockey sticks laid cross-checks on the likes of Bud Cort and Chris Rock in Kevin Smith’s Dogma . The enforcer in the blue Highlands Clamdiggers jersey? That was Kitao Sakurai , a teenage actor based in Cleveland at the time. He couldn’t have known it then, but his role in Smith’s slacker-minded religious satire offered an early glimpse of the offbeat sensibility he’d later bring to his own filmmaking — a sensibility now on full display in Street Fighter , the number-one movie in America.

Fueled by the Cleveland Cinematheque’s programming diet of Jackie Chan, Jet Li and Robert Altman, young Sakurai grew just as interested in working behind the camera. By 19, he’d dropped out of college and moved to New York to give independent filmmaking a go. He got his start as a music video cinematographer before crossing paths with Eric André on a shoot in the mid-2000s. Related Stories Movies Brad Pitt's 'Cliff Booth' Reveals Action-Packed Scenes in New Tease Ahead of Netflix Launch Movies 'You Can See Everything' Triumphs With $15M as 'Street Fighter' Wins Weekend

Impressed by Sakurai’s eye for vintage gear and aesthetics, André quickly hit it off with the aspiring filmmaker. A few years later, the two teamed up to develop a proof of concept for The Eric Andre Show . But selling the chaotic “anti-talk show” proved difficult, with networks passing on the project one after another. Resigned to releasing it themselves on YouTube, Sakurai and André were stunned when Cartoon Network’s Adult Swim took a flyer on the series in 2010. Since then, it’s spawned 60 episodes, several specials and an Emmy win.

That same year, Sakurai premiered his feature directorial debut, Aardvark (2010). The experimental film fictionalized the real-life relationship between Larry Lewis Jr., a blind recovering alcoholic, and his jiu-jitsu instructor, Darren Branch, before pivoting from docu-narrative to revenge thriller.

While Aardvark hinted at Sakurai’s appetite for the unconventional, The Eric Andre Show pushed that instinct further, cementing an approach that continues to inform his work. As long as absurdity is embraced wholeheartedly, it doesn’t always need to adhere to conventional logic or narrative coherence to work.

“Sometimes things don’t necessarily need to make sense for you to lean in and love them,” Sakurai tells The Hollywood Reporter . “There can be elements that are so ridiculous they might not track narratively or make sense conceptually, but because they’re part of an overall energy and feeling, they fit.”

entertainment.title: How Lil Jon’s Almost 2-Year-Old Daughter Helped After the Loss of His Son: ‘She Was Able to Warm Me Up With Her Love’
entertainment.summary: The Atlanta producer makes an appearance on ABC News' Nightline to promote his new memoir I Only Shout So You Can Hear Me .
entertainment.body:
Lil Jon stopped by ABC’s Nightline to promote his recently released memoir I Only Shout So You Can Hear Me and touched on some pretty emotional topics.

While speaking with ABC News correspondent Stephanie Ramos for Wednesday night’s (Oct. 21) episode, the Atlanta producer talked about how he felt when he found out that the father that raised him wasn’t his biological father.

“You know, I can’t go back and ask my father that raised me, ‘Did you know?’ It’s so many unanswered questions, and it just beats you up,” Jon says in a preview clip exclusively on Billboard . “And then you go through an array of emotions, of anger to frustration to sadness to doubt to … you don’t — it’s just everything you go through, and it’s just like your life is not what you thought your life is. And then it’s also like, well, what would my life have been like if I did know my other father? What would he have taught me? Or what would I have learned?”

He also spoke on losing his 27-year-old son , Nathan Smith, in an accidental drowning this past February while he was in the middle of writing this book and how his almost 2-year-old daughter Nahara helped numb the pain. ”I didn’t realize I was gonna go through life-changing things while I was writing this book, like the loss of my son,” he said. “So, I think it was all divine timing with this book happening because these stories needed to be told.

“It’s been rough,” he added. “It’s been hard. It’s a bunch of things that have helped me get through it, like my daughter. You know, my daughter is almost 2 years old now, and, you know, having part of me ripped out of my chest, she was able to help to repair some of that. When I was cold, she was able to warm me up with her love.”

Nightline airs at 12:35 a.m. ET on ABC with episodes available to stream the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

entertainment.title: Aaron Carter Estate Settles With Walgreens in Wrongful Death Lawsuit Over Xanax Prescriptions
entertainment.summary: The late singer’s family has resolved their claims against Walgreens and another Los Angeles pharmacy. They’re still suing his former dentist.
entertainment.body:
The estate of Aaron Carter has settled wrongful death claims against Walgreens and another pharmacy that filled the singer’s Xanax prescriptions before his 2022 drowning.

Attorneys for Carter’s family announced in a Thursday (Oct. 15) court filing, obtained and first reported by Billboard , that they’ve “reached a settlement resolving all claims” against both Walgreens and Santa Monica Medical Plaza Pharmacy. The estate still has claims remaining against a dentist that prescribed Xanax to the 2000s pop star.

Deal terms were not made public. The Carter estate’s attorney, Marc Lazo , told Billboard on Wednesday (Oct. 21) that they’re “satisfied” with the settlement. “We’re pleased that the pharmaceutical parties have accepted a resolution,” added Lazo. “It took some time to get there, but we did it.”

Reps for Walgreens and Santa Monica Medical did not return requests for comment.

Carter drowned in a bathtub at the age of 34 with drugs in his system. In 2023, his former fiancée brought a wrongful death lawsuit on behalf of their four-year-old son alleging a psychiatrist and dentist were to blame for overprescribing Xanax to Carter, and that pharmacies wrongly filled the prescriptions without checking to see if he was abusing the drug.

The defendants all maintained that Carter’s death was caused not by Xanax, but by the gas he inhaled from canisters of compressed air (known as difluoroethane). In court filings, they argued that the amount of Xanax in Carter’s system at the time of death was not enough to make him lose consciousness.

The psychiatry clinic was the first to settle with Carter’s family this past May. The pharmacies have now followed suit, though dentist Jason Mirabile is still fighting the claims. Mirabile is currently scheduled to go to trial against the Carter estate in January.

Mirabile’s attorneys have indicated in pre-trial filings that they plan to argue Carter was an absentee father to his son, and that therefore, the child cannot win damages for lost financial support or companionship. Mirabile’s team wants to call witnesses from the Department of Children and Family Services, who allegedly got involved in a custody dispute between Carter and his former fiancée before he died.

Nicki Minaj’s MAGA pivot won’t be ending anytime soon. Minaj informed the Barbz via X on Tuesday (Oct. 20) that she’s “not going anywhere” when it comes to her political allegiances and loyalty to President Donald Trump.

“Not going anywhere. Right where I need to be,” Minaj added on X hours later.

The Queens native served as a judge for the Trump administration’s small-business Million Dollar Pitch Competition, which had a $1 million prize on the line. She was joined by private equity fund manager Grant Cardone and Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia as judges for the competition.

Minaj hasn’t been shy about her ties to the Republican Party and praise for Donald Trump throughout the year. The “Super Bass” rapper met the president for the frist time at a Trump Accounts Summit in January, where she labeled herself as his No. 1 fan.

The commander in chief returned the favor while championing Minaj during a presidential luncheon in July. “She’s a fantastic person and she’s a woman that’s respected by everybody,” he said. “And she’s got real talent, Nicki Minaj. Nicki, stand up, please. Such a great person and respected by everybody.”

Nicki Minaj continued her love affair with the Trump administration during a September appearance on The Ingraham Angle . “I am honored to be able to have an opportunity to work with this administration and to work with President Trump. He has inspired many people, not just me. He’s fun,” Minaj said.

While her Trump support has turned off some of her Barbz and collaborators, Cyndi Lauper doesn’t regret working with Minaj. entertainment.title: This ‘Glee’ Star Is Ready to Reclaim Hot 100 Record From Drake: ‘Challenge Accepted’
entertainment.summary: One commenter marveled: "the concept of the glee cast re-assembling like the avengers just to dethrone drake."
entertainment.body:
Back in January 2020, when Drake tied the Glee cast’s record for notching the most Billboard Hot 100 entries ever, he posted a selfie video in which he says directly to camera: “One more to go. Gleeful!”

Now, with Wednesday’s (Oct. 21) news of a Glee reboot coming to Disney+ and Hulu , one Gleek is ready for the New Directions to reclaim their record.

The day the reboot news was announced, Glee star Kevin McHale — who played Artie Abrams on the show — took to X and quote-tweeted a Genius post from that fateful day in January 2020 that announced “drake has officially passed the cast of ‘glee’ and now has the most billboard hot 100 hits of all time.”

The top responses harkened back to the heyday of both Twitter and Glee itself, with Tyler Oakley chiming in: “this being how i found out.” Meanwhile, Mike O’Malley — who played Kurt Hummel’s dad Burt on the original Fox series — asked, “Can I finally sing something now?!!!” Another commenter asked, “how long have you had this draft saved my god.”

Another quote-tweet marveled : “the concept of the glee cast re-assembling like the avengers just to dethrone drake.”

Of course, the Glee cast is going to have their work cut out for them, given more than a decade has transpired since the original series went off the air in 2015 and a lot more contenders have emerged in the years after. Since tying the Glee record of 207 Hot 100 entries in 2020, Drake now stands at a whopping 407. Not only that, but two other artists stand between the Glee cast and Drake: Taylor Swift with 281 and Future with 246.

Out of those 207 Hot 100 entries, the Glee cast scored three top 10 hits during the series’ original 2009-2015 run: “Don’t Stop Believin'” in 2009 (No. 4 peak), “Loser Like Me” in 2011 (No. 6 peak), and “Teenage Dream” in 2010 (No. 8 peak).

The reboot news arrived first thing Wednesday, with the message “Currently gleeking out!” splashed across social media.

entertainment.title: AI-Generated Music and the Future of Creativity Discussed at Billboard Latin Music Week
entertainment.summary: Experts talk about the challenges authors face, and whether regulation is enough, in the era of artificial intelligence.
entertainment.body:
While many regions and countries already have regulations in place, Spain has expressed “concerns” about AI “completely replacing” human creators. Cristina Perpiñá-Robert , director general of the Spanish Society of Authors and Publishers (SGAE), voiced this concern on Tuesday (Oct. 20) during a discussion on AI-generated music and the future of creativity at Billboard Latin Music Week. She called for regulations to protect creators.

“In the U.S., we’re taking an approach in favor of technology and AI. I think it’s the same in Europe,” Perpiñá-Robert said. “The thing is, you know, creators and music creators we’re seeing in Spain, they are using AI. They’re enhancing AI (…) Our biggest concern is not so much the licensing process. It’s the fact that the content which is generated with AI is completely replacing human creators. That’s our concern”.

During the panel, moderated by MIDiA Research’s vp of music strategy, Tatiana Cirisano , and featuring Pierre Hachar Jr. , managing partner of The Hachar Law Group, Perpiñá-Robert stated that Spain is concerned that regulation “is not enough,” as creators and authors are being “completely excluded” from the business model. “It’s not only how to license the model, it’s how to prevent creators from not being hired anymore because you can just resort to synthetic music,” she added.

The risk of powerful AI models bypassing human control and harming humanity has become a more pressing concern. In the U.S., President Donald Trump reportedly rejected halting AI development over fears that China could gain an advantage in the technology, according to the Associated Press .

Hachar Jr. revealed that most of his clients are already using AI. “Whether they wanna admit it or not, they’re using AI. Some of them are not, but they’re genius-level songwriters and producers and artists that don’t need to use AI, frankly”.

The executive emphasized that technology always helps foster growth, “whether we like it or not.” He noted that when streaming first emerged, people were resistant to it, but now it’s commonplace. The same happened with production tools like Pro Tools, Reason, Logic and FL Studio.

“[Many said:] ‘Oh, it’s the end of the musician!’ Well, no, it’s the start of a whole new group of people that can explore creativity, right? And that’s the way I see AI,” he said.

entertainment.body:
Third time was a charm for Billie Eilish and Finneas as the music superstars picked up record-setting song of the year honors for their track “Wildflower” at the 2026 Grammy Awards . The trophy marked a third song of the year victory following wins for “Bad Guy” in 2020, and “What Was I Made For” in 2024.”

But “Wildflower” has new life beyond the other two as the hit-making siblings leaned on it for inspiration for another new project: the Billie Eilish & Finneas Collection for John Hardy , a luxury handcrafted jewelry brand founded in Bali, Indonesia, by the Canadian artist in 1975. The line comes after Eilish and Finneas were appointed as creative partners for John Hardy last year, but the new range marks the first they co-designed. Per intel from John Hardy, the collection was developed over the past year with the house’s New York and Bali-based design teams under the creative direction of Reed Krakoff. Related Stories Anatomy of a Hit Song "Where Is My Husband!" Inside the Song That Made Raye All The Rage Lifestyle Finneas O'Connell and Claudia Sulewski Are Married

The collection reflects their shared sensibilities around creativity and sustainability with a focus on handcrafted, modern designs using responsible materials like reclaimed metals, lab grown diamonds and production facilities powered by 100 percent renewable energy. To promote the line, the brother-sister duo posed for Trey Laird, who used grainy Super-8 film to capture them in a room filled with flowers, shifting lights and shadows, seen below.

“Jewelry has always been an enormous part of how I express myself. It’s such an important reflection of a certain time in your life,” said Eilish. “In my current day-to-day, I wear daintier jewelry. On tour, I love a chunkier, thicker piece. I love that we were able to work with both styles.” Added Finneas, aka Finneas O’Connell: “As we’ve grown and evolved, Billie and I have become more minimalistic in our taste. Sometimes the simplest silhouette is the thing I appreciate the most.”

Krakoff also noted that they both brought “very distinct” points of view to the design process. “From the beginning, they challenged us to think differently about the tension between softness and strength, symmetry and balance. The result feels personal to Billie and Finneas and unmistakably John Hardy,” she said.

entertainment.body:
Agushto Papá, Juancito & Jess Judith gathered at the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Week to discuss the new wave of podcasters and its impact on music.

During a conversation moderated by Billboard Español’s Isabela Raygoza, each speaker revealed why they decided to become podcasters. “I never thought I’d end up working in social media—I’m a marketing major—but my content has always just been a reflection of who I am, plain and simple,” Judith, a Dominican influencer-turned-podcaster said. “I love music, and it’s been wild to see the journey of how it went from being my passion to becoming my job.” Related 'Nothing Short of Extraordinary': Powderfinger Pledges Encore Dates After Reunion Tour Sells Out Billboard & Maybelline Announce Partnership to Elevate Artists at Latin Music Week 2026 Charli xcx Cancels Arizona Concert, Says 'It Breaks Me' to Miss It Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

“My podcast is called ‘Desde Cero’ (From Scratch),” Venezuelan podcaster Juancito shared. “I used to work in Uber and construction, and it was during those jobs that I started writing down ideas and wanting to conduct interviews. Everyone starts from scratch, and seven years later, we have a residency in Miami with a live audience.”

As for Agushto Papá—a Música Mexicana project composed of Diego Mondragon, Angel Lopez, and Jason Nuñez—the three childhood friends decided to launch their podcast when they didn’t have luck as a sierreño group.

“We’re music fans, and we felt there was a disconnect when we started,” Mondragon noted. “All of a sudden all of these artists were reaching the charts, and not a lot of people were covering them. It wasn’t a plan, but we were able to connect the fans from the U.S. that listen to Mexican music to the artist.”

As for what’s the role that podcasters play in a music artist’s career?

Judith explained: “People want to see something different and get to know you—not what someone else is doing. The difference between short-form and long-form content is that people connect more deeply; they’re interested in watching something longer. The coolest part is sitting down with these people and asking them about everything that’s going on.”

“I understood what we have to offer them,” Juancito added. “What do I bring to their promotion? What do you have to offer the artist? Do you have a strategy that adds value to their promotion? Right now, there is such a massive saturation of content that we really need to stand out.”

Grupo Duelo celebrated one of the most important years of their career during the 2026 Billboard Latin Music Week .

On Tuesday (Oct. 20), Oscar Iván Treviño sat down with Tere Aguilera, Billboard ‘s Mexico correspondent, for a “Milestone Moment” presented by La Bonita Music, before joining his bandmates to perform their latest single and receive a commemorative plaque honoring their chart achievements.

The recognition highlighted the two No. 1s the group achieved this year on the Regional Mexican Airplay chart with “Te Cura el Tiempo” and “Para Que a No Duela,” both songs from their album Gravedad . During the conversation, Treviño spoke about how Duelo helped modernize norteño music by incorporating a more romantic approach and experimenting with different rhythms. “We made [norteño] music more romantic and played around with the genre a bit more,” he explained, referencing songs like “Malabares” and “Veneno.” Traditional norteño music is experiencing a renewed surge.

The singer also emphasized the importance of representing the culture of northern Mexico and southern Texas, an identity he described as the union of two cultures. The son of migrant parents, Treviño recalled working in the fields of the United States before establishing his music career. “It’s an honor to carry it with great pride and say that I’m a Mexican living in the U.S.,” he said about norteño music.

“Norteño music has deep roots, originating from the cantinas where it was played and over time, it has evolved and modernized,” the frontman added. “It’s a fundamental part of our community and our society.”

This year also marked Duelo’s return to a traditional label structure after years as an independent act under La Bonita Music. In February, the group signed a partnership with Warner Music and, alongside Live Nation, embarked on their first arena tour across the United States and Mexico. The band celebrated three sold-out shows at Houston’s Toyota Center and still had several dates remaining to wrap up their Gravedad Tour.

“Mexican music is a culture with many roots,” he said. “It’s a beautiful thing to represent all our people.” After receiving the plaque, the six members of Grupo Duelo took to the stage to continue the celebration with a live performance.

The Penguin creator and showrunner Lauren LeFranc is in talks to produce a series on the super-villain for HBO and DC Studios , The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. No cast or writer specifics are yet available for the series, which is in early stages, though it‘s said that the series would not fall within The Batman director Matt Reeves’ universe for the character.

Deadline was the first to report the news. HBO declined to comment. Related Stories Movies 'Clayface' Reviews Roundup: From "a Stroke of Brilliance" to "Messy DC Miss" Movies 'Clayface' Review: DC Studios' Batman Villain Origin Story Is a Bona Fide Body-Horror Delight

In the world of Batman comics, Poison Ivy is the alter ego of Dr. Pamela Isley, a botanist who gains supernatural powers to control plants and subsequently becomes an ecoterrorist in Gotham. After her introduction in the comics in 1966, she became a staple of the superhero’s rogues gallery, later to be memorably portrayed by Uma Thurman in the 1997 live-action film Batman & Robin .

Poison Ivy has never fronted her own television series, though she’s starred frequently in animated projects like Batman: The Animated Series , Batman: The Brave and the Bold and Harley Quinn (the character to which she is sometimes romantically linked). She also made appearances in the live-action series Gotham and Batwoman .

LeFranc, meanwhile, made her mark on Gotham with The Penguin , which became a ratings hit and a critical darling when it debuted in 2024. That series was firmly within Reeves’ Batman universe, with Colin Farrell reprising his prosthetics-heavy role from The Batman as the eponymous villain and Reeves serving as an executive producer. The series won nine Emmys in 2025.

Prior to The Penguin , LeFranc worked with Marvel as a writer and producer on ABC’s Agents of SHIELD .

The news arrives just a day before a lesser-known Batman villain, Clayface , gets the silver-screen treatment with his eponymous film directed by James Watkins. The next installment in Reeves‘ Batman film series, The Batman Part II , is slated to premiere on Feb. 18, 2028. Meanwhile, HBO has not renewed The Penguin for a second season.

entertainment.title: ‘Clayface’ Reviews Roundup: From “a Stroke of Brilliance” to “Messy DC Miss”
entertainment.summary: Director James Watkins' DC horror film is getting largely positive reviews, though with a fair share of detractors.
entertainment.body:
Logo text Here’s the very good news: Reviews for Clayface are generally positive, and out of the gate, the film has a much higher Rotten Tomatoes score than DC’s last effort, Supergirl (around 74 percent positive instead of 52 percent).

As a stand-alone body horror story set in the DC world, director James Watkins ( Speak No Evil ) is said to largely succeed in pulling off the story of Matt Hagen — a rising Hollywood actor from Gotham City whose career is destroyed when a crime boss brutally disfigures his face, prompting him to undergo an experimental procedure that turns him into a shapeshifter. Even detractors say star Tom Rhys Harries is terrific in his major leading role debut , and praise the film’s use of practical effects. Related Stories Movies 'Clayface' Review: DC Studios' Batman Villain Origin Story Is a Bona Fide Body-Horror Delight Movies DC Studios' James Gunn and Peter Safran Recall Detailing Long-Term Plans to New Boss David Ellison

And with a modest, by superhero movie standards, $40 million budget, the film doesn’t need to be a blockbuster to turn a profit when it opens Friday (it’s projected to open north of $20 million, up against some surprise competition from the documentary You Can See Everything ).

The film has its share of detractors, too, with some criticizing the film — with its script by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini — for being a rather predictable revenge thriller that doesn’t do anything with its Gotham City location.

The Hollywood Reporte r : “ Clayface emerges as one of the year’s big surprises … With its grimy visuals and pulpy dialogue redolent of comic books in the most evocative way, Clayface delivers the sort of psychological depth and emotional resonance that enable it to bear comparisons to the works of such body horror maestros as David Cronenberg and Sam Raimi.”

USA Today : “A messy DC miss … While Harries gives a complicated human touch to all the assorted versions of Matt’s internal strife and external facade (boosted by some excellent effects work), Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini’s screenplay does almost nothing with him as a character … Clayface also is the one Batman-adjacent project that, strangely, doesn’t utilize Gotham itself as a character.”

The Telegraph : “Director James Watkins, of Eden Lake and The Woman in Black , has crafted a stylish and stomach-twisting, contemporary, urban, body horror inspired by vintage material that just so happens to be a DC superhero title. There is no pandering to fans, nor gestures towards grander unfolding narratives … It cannot be overstated how much fun it is to soak up a film like this on what feels like its creators’ largely unhindered terms. Aside from the occasional reference to Gotham City, in fact, you could feasibly leave a screening of Clayface with no idea you’d been watching a franchise movie.”

entertainment.title: Netflix Is Searching For Its Next Big Story. The Protagonist? Itself
entertainment.summary: The streaming company has controlled its message for years, now it is hunting for what will pique Wall Street's interest.
entertainment.body:
Netflix is in the storytelling business, but it seems to have lost the plot on perhaps the most interesting story it needs to be telling: Its own.

That may be at the heart of the stunning shake up at the company over the last week, which saw content chief Bela Bejaria, film head Dan Lin and 1,000 or so other employees let go in a plan to refocus the company’s content under new hire Peter Rice.

To understand what’s going on requires you to understand Netflix’s unique (at least for the media business) ability to tell its story to Wall Street, and to do so in a way that valued the company as though it were a tech titan like Google or Apple. Netflix was once part of the legendary group of FAANG stocks that drove stock market growth for years.

Once it began its pursuit of Warner Bros. last year, however, Wall Street got spooked. All of sudden Netflix is being valued more like a traditional media company, rather than a high-flying tech company.

Why else would Netflix so fully be willing to embrace theatrical movies or be willing to take on linear assets like HBO or TCM?

On the company’s latest earnings call, co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters insisted that their strategy wasn’t changing, but it doesn’t take much reading between the lines to see that even if the topline strategy is the same (“We want to be the must-have entertainment service, the first one members check for a great series or a great film, and the last service they would ever cancel”), there are changes being made at the margins.

That means doubling down in some areas, like high-quality originals built for the U.S. domestic market, “where we can have an outsized impact when we create a big buzzy show that members love and talk about all over the world,” Sarandos said.

And it will mean more sports and live events, which Sarandos noted really “break through.”
